ber_001: You can recognise it by the gnarled, hollow trunk close to six metres round, on a tree only 15 to 16 metres tall. It stands in the open Tegel Forest at An der Malche, outside the Schlosspark where the thicker Humboldt Oak grows.
ber_002: You can recognise it by the trunk, 7.80 metres round, the widest in Berlin, under a crown spanning 18 metres. It stands inside the grounds of Schloss Tegel, past the donation gate, a few hundred metres from Dicke Marie.
ber_003: You can recognise it by the weathered trunk, around 6.70 metres round, and the thinned upper crown left by lightning. It stands at the Große Steinlanke inlet on the Havel, signed from the Großes Fenster clearing.
ber_004: You can recognise it by the conifer that drops all its needles each winter, on a trunk five metres round. It stands in the looser English section of Schlosspark Charlottenburg, about a hundred metres from the carp pond elm.
ber_005: You can recognise it by the trunk, 6.35 metres round under a 25 metre crown, growing with its roots straight into the Spree bank. It stands near the Rosengarten in Treptower Park, a short walk from the boat landing.
ber_006: You can recognise it by the squat, hollowed crown barely topping the church roof and by the steel cables bracing its limbs. It stands on public ground in front of the old parish church on Hönower Straße, behind a low fence.
ber_007: You can recognise it by the branches grown together into single fused limbs, on a trunk 4.65 metres round and 25 metres tall. It stands inside the Tierpark, the oldest tree on the old Friedrichsfelde palace grounds.
ber_008: You can recognise it by the plaque at its foot marking 125 years since the first Kaisereiche was planted. It stands alone on the street corner where Rheinstraße meets Moselstraße, at the bus stop that carries its name.
ber_009: You can recognise it by the uniform gold it turns in late October, every leaf at once. It stands in the free Gutspark behind Schloss Britz, over three metres round and close to 20 metres, the largest ginkgo in Berlin.
ber_010: You can recognise it by the bulk of it, the heaviest conifer in the Tiergarten and among the tallest trees in Berlin. It stands in the Englischer Garten section near Altonaer Straße, a short walk from Schloss Bellevue.
ber_013: You can recognise it by the wide crown branching low over the path. It stands north of the Wasservogelteich, the waterfowl pond, about a kilometre deeper into Pfaueninsel than the island's other two registered oaks.
ber_014: You can recognise it as the one plane among Pfaueninsel's registered trees, and the only one on the mainland side of the water. It stands beside the Wirtshaus zur Pfaueninsel at Pfaueninselchaussee 100, by the ferry dock.
ber_015: You can recognise it by the deeply cut, almost fern-like leaves, unlike the plain oval leaf of every other oak on the island. It stands forty five metres from the Great Oak, roughly 150 metres northeast of the Schloss.
ber_016: You can recognise it by the single trunk, 6.43 metres round and 22 metres tall, the sixth thickest tree recorded in Berlin. It stands on the north shore of the Lietzensee, about 170 metres along the path from the wingnut.
ber_017: You can recognise it by the trunk splitting into several stems close to the ground, so it reads as a small grove on one root plate. It stands in the northeast corner of Lietzenseepark, 170 metres from the single-trunked plane.
ber_018: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.88 metres round and 21.5 metres tall, on an elm where most of Europe's big elms are gone. It stands at the southeastern corner of the carp pond behind Charlottenburg Palace.
ber_020: You can recognise it by being the only tree on the whole Olympiastadion site, 810 metres by 320 and otherwise bare. It stands behind the Preussenturm at the Osttor, visible from outside the fence.
